questions.q: State Aristotle's law of motion in your own words and give one everyday example that seems to support it.
questions.a: Aristotle's law: "An external force is required to keep a body in motion." Example: A child must continuously pull a toy car with a string to keep it moving on the floor; if the child stops pulling, the car stops. A wrong answer (e.g., "force is needed to start motion only") reveals the student has not grasped the historical misconception that dominated physics for nearly two millennia.

questions.q: Why did Aristotle—and most people—believe a force is needed to sustain uniform motion? Identify the specific force that is always present in terrestrial experience but absent in Galileo's idealised thought experiment.
questions.a: Aristotle generalised from everyday experience where friction (and air resistance) always opposes motion. On Earth, a moving object slows down unless a force counters friction. Galileo's genius was to imagine a world without friction—an idealised horizontal plane—where no force is needed to maintain uniform motion. A wrong answer (e.g., "gravity stops the motion") reveals confusion between the vertical force of gravity and the horizontal retarding force of friction.

questions.q: A ball is released from rest at height h on a smooth (frictionless) inclined plane. It rolls down and up a second smooth inclined plane of the same angle. What maximum height does it reach on the second plane? Now, if the second plane is made horizontal (angle = 0°), how far does the ball travel before stopping? Explain using energy reasoning.
questions.a: On the second inclined plane, the ball reaches exactly height h (conservation of mechanical energy, no friction). On a horizontal plane (angle = 0°), the ball never stops—it travels an infinite distance at constant speed because no component of gravity acts horizontally and there is no friction to dissipate kinetic energy. A wrong answer (e.g., "it stops after a finite distance") reveals the student still thinks motion naturally decays without friction.

questions.q: Galileo's double inclined plane experiment is often called a "thought experiment." Why could Galileo not perform this experiment exactly as described in a real laboratory? What practical limitation forces the ball to stop even on a horizontal plane?
questions.a: In a real laboratory, friction (rolling friction, air resistance) can never be completely eliminated. Even on a very smooth horizontal surface, these dissipative forces do negative work, reducing the ball's kinetic energy until it stops. Galileo's experiment is a thought experiment because it requires an idealised frictionless world that does not exist. A wrong answer (e.g., "gravity pulls it down") shows the student does not distinguish between vertical and horizontal forces.

questions.q: A student argues: "Galileo was wrong. If I stop pushing my bicycle on a level road, it stops. So force IS needed to keep it moving." Evaluate this claim. Is the student's observation correct? Is the conclusion correct? Explain the flaw in reasoning.
questions.a: The observation is correct (bicycle stops), but the conclusion is wrong. The bicycle stops because friction (tyre-road, bearings, air resistance) exerts a net retarding force. To maintain constant velocity, the cyclist must apply a forward force that exactly cancels friction—net force zero. Galileo's law states: if net external force is zero, velocity is constant. The student confuses "applied force" with "net force." A wrong evaluation (e.g., "student is right because bicycle stops") reveals failure to distinguish individual forces from net force.

questions.q: Design a simple classroom demonstration using low-cost materials (e.g., a wooden plank, a marble, a towel, a book) that illustrates Galileo's insight: reducing friction makes an object move farther with the same initial push. Describe the setup, the variable you change, and what students should observe.
questions.a: Setup: Place a wooden plank at a slight incline. Release a marble from a fixed height on three surfaces: (1) bare wood, (2) wood covered with a towel, (3) wood with a smooth plastic sheet (or just the bare wood if very smooth). Variable: surface roughness (friction coefficient). Observation: Marble travels farthest on smoothest surface. Students infer: less friction → less opposing force → longer distance at constant speed on horizontal. A poor answer (e.g., "use a fan to blow the marble") misses the point of varying friction while keeping initial energy the same.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Aristotle's fallacy is the incorrect assertion that a continuous external force is required to maintain a body in uniform motion; Galileo's experiments with inclined planes demonstrated that in the absence of friction, a body in uniform motion continues ______ without any external force, establishing the law of inertia: a body remains in its state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line unless compelled by a net external force to change that state.
Fill in the blank: Observe a marble rolling on a smooth floor versus a rough carpet—on the smooth floor it travels farther before ______.
What is Aristotle's fallacy? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Aristotle's fallacy is the incorrect assertion that a continuous external force is required to maintain a body in uniform motion; Galileo's experiments with inclined planes demonstrated that in the absence of friction, a body in uniform motion continues indefinitely without any external force, establishing the law of inertia: a body.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Aristotle's fallacy?
questions.a: Students believe "inertia is a force that keeps things moving" or "inertia is the tendency to resist motion." In reality, inertia is a property of mass—it is the resistance to *change* in velocity (both starting and stopping).

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain why Aristotle's view was a natural but flawed interpretation of everyday experience, describe Galileo's double inclined plane thought experiment and its logical conclusion, and articulate why friction—not a fundamental property of motion—is the reason objects stop on Earth.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Aristotle's fallacy is the incorrect assertion that a continuous external force is required to maintain a body in uniform motion; Galileo's experiments with inclined planes ______ that in the absence of friction, a body in uniform motion continues indefinitely without any external force, establishing the law of inertia: a body remains in its state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line unless compelled by a net external force to change that state.
